items.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar Says She Will ‘Not Be Silenced’ After Federal Agents Raid Her Home
items.standfirst: Democratic leaders have condemned the raid on Omar’s home as "deeply disturbing."
items.content: Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 12, 2026. —Andrew Leyden—Getty ImagesDemocratic Representative Ilhan ‌Omar of Minnesota on Monday afternoon called the federal agents’ search of her Washington, D.C. home an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” The Somali-born lawmaker is a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has previously been subjected to his insults.“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” said Omar in a social media post. “I will not be silenced.”A spokesperson for the Department of Justice told TIME: “Today in the Washington, D.C, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” No further details were provided.The U.S. Congress is currently not in session and it is unclear if Omar was home at the time of the search.Omar's office denounced the raid as "an outrageous abuse of power" and said the "Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."According to Reuters, a person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork that was filled out by her late father when she was a child.TIME has reached out to the White House and Omar’s office for further information.While the reason behind the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time Omar’s immigration records have become a focal point. Earlier this year, Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of records pertaining to Omar, who gained her U.S. citizenship in 2000, when she was 17.In a podcast interview in March, Vice President J.D. Vance, without offering evidence, said "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against" the United States. Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.Last month, White House border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was the subject of an "ongoing criminal investigation," but declined to offer specific details.Trump says he had "nothing to do with" raidHours after the search, Trump suggested he was not involved in the investigation and referred to Omar as "crooked" and "terrible." “Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters outside the White House. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”He added: “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ [Department of Justice]. I have nothing to do with it.”Democrats condemn raid on Omar’s homeThe raid was carried out just over three weeks ​before the midterm elections, in which the Republicans will grapple to maintain control of the House and Senate. Omar is seeking a fifth two-year term in the House of Representatives.Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz led Democrats in denouncing the raid, saying “Americans see this for what it is—President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries referred to the raid as “deeply disturbing” and argued that it raises “serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government” against Trump’s adversaries."Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," he said in a statement, which was co-signed by House minority whip Rep. Katherine Clark and Rep. Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus.The Justice Department has historically avoided federal prosecutors indicting a candidate or federal law enforcement taking "overt" investigative steps regarding a candidate—such as executing a search warrant—within 60 days of a primary or general election.Rep. Ro Khanna of California referred to the raid as a "disturbing" development and implored "any decent American" to "stand up and speak out."Rep. Robert Garcia, also of California and the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said the search is an "outrageous escalation in the President's continued weaponization of our government against anyone who dares to stand up to him."He added: "Searching a Representative's home over a decades-old immigration filing by her father is an authoritarian abuse of power. No family deserves these continued attacks."Trump has previously been accused of targeting his political opponents.Last year, he called on former Attorney General Pam Bondi to begin prosecuting California Sen. Adam Schiff, a Democrat, former FBI Director James Comey, and New York Attorney General Letitia James, all of whom led investigations into Trump, political or criminal.James was charged with mortgage fraud by the Justice Department last year, but a federal judge dismissed the case. James denied the allegations.In April, a federal grand jury indicted Comey over a social media post that the Trump Administration characterized as a threat against the President. Comey said he was "innocent" and vowed to fight the case, which has been delayed until early 2027.Rep. Ilhan Omar speaks to members of the media following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. on July 15, 2026. —Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg—Getty ImagesOmar has accused Trump of having a “weird” obsession with herTrump has long targeted Omar and her birthplace Somalia during his anti-immigration speeches and remarks. He has repeatedly pointed to well-documented instances of “fraud” in Minnesota involving people of Somali ancestry and welfare programs, seemingly blaming the community as a whole rather than the individuals involved.Last December, while delivering an address in Pennsylvania, Trump referenced Omar during an anti-immigration tirade, claiming she does “nothing but b-tch” and arguing that she comes from a county considered to be “the worst” in the world. “We ought to get her the hell out,” the President said, pausing as members of the crowd chanted “send her back.”Omar at the time responded by saying Trump’s “obsession” with her is “beyond weird.”“Since he has no economic policies to tout, he’s resorting to regurgitating bigoted lies instead,” said Omar via social media, reacting to a clip of the President’s speech. “He continues to be a national embarrassment.”In January, Omar was approached by a man with a syringe during a Town Hall meeting in Minneapolis. The man sprayed her with a substance before being restrained by on-site security. Lab analysis later determined the liquid contained acetic acid and identified it as a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. Last month, a 56-year-old man named Anthony James Kazmierczak was sentenced to 14 months in prison for the assault. Shortly after the Town Hall incident, Omar called out Trump’s use of “hateful rhetoric” against her and suggested he had made her a target.“What the facts have shown, since I’ve gotten into elected office, is that every time the President of the United States has chosen to use hateful rhetoric to talk about me and the community that I represent, my death threats skyrocket,” she said. “I wouldn’t be where I am at today, having to pay for security, having the government to think about providing me security, if Donald Trump wasn’t in office and if he wasn’t so obsessed with me."

items.standfirst: The Trump Administration is reportedly considering firing the ambassador to Greece after alleged improper conduct.
items.content: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks during a dedication ceremony at the chancery of the U.S. Embassy in Athens, on Oct. 7, 2026. —Mark Schiefelbein—Pool/AFP/Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump is reportedly considering dismissing the U.S. ambassador to Greece, former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr. Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of alleged misconduct before and during her tenure in Athens.The Associated Press and CNN, citing unnamed sources, said that a decision on Guilfoyle is expected soon. A senior U.S. official told the AP on Sunday that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely assess future action after the Monday U.S. holiday.The controversy emerged in late September, when the Wall Street Journal began publishing a series of reports about Guilfoyle’s questionable activities—including promoting a Greek construction firm, bragging about luxury trips paid for by businessmen, and asking a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for getting the attention of the Trump Administration.The State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, the AP and the Journal reported. TIME has reached out to the White House and the State Department for comment, as well as a lawyer for Guilfoyle.The reports surfaced around Rubio’s multiple-day visit to Europe last week, when the Secretary of State boasted about the Trump Administration’s achievements and Guilfoyle attended most of his events in Athens. When asked about the reports on Oct. 8, Rubio at first appeared incredulous, telling journalists: “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true. You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me.”As the reports emerged, Trump did not defend Guilfoyle, who was in a relationship with his eldest son between 2018 and 2024. “I just heard about it—too bad,” the President told reporters on Friday. “I mean, I don’t know. She’s an ambassador. I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much. She was always very nice.”Vice President J.D. Vance reserved comment on the reporting around Guilfoyle, though he said Thursday that he does not like “anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” and added the next day that “if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it.”Here’s what to know.Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle?Trump announced he would nominate Guilfoyle to be the U.S. ambassador to Greece in December 2024, just before the start of his second term and amid reports of her split with Trump Jr. She was sworn in in September 2025, becoming the first woman in the role. The 57-year-old Guilfoyle was a former prosecutor in the San Francisco and Los Angeles District Attorney’s Offices and was appointed Assistant District Attorney in San Francisco in 2000. She gained fame as a co-host of the Fox News’ conservative political talk show The Five, which she joined in 2011 and left in 2018.Besides Guilfoyle’s legal and media work, she also helped raise funds for Trump’s presidential campaign in 2020. Guilfoyle was also a witness to the events leading up to the Jan. 6, 2021 U.S. Capitol attack, and met with the House committee investigating the insurrection in 2022.From 2001 to 2006, Guilfoyle was married to Gavin Newsom, then a San Francisco supervisor and later mayor and now California’s governor who’s widely seen as a Democratic presidential contender. What has been reported about Guilfoyle?On Sept. 25, the Journal published a report on Guilfoyle promoting the Greek construction firm Aktor Group and having the company’s lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, attend diplomatic meetings across Balkan states. Guilfoyle reportedly encouraged governments from Bulgaria to Albania to work with Aktor Group.The Sept. 25 report also detailed Guilfoyle’s alleged behavior with Greek government officials. According to the Journal report, during a March dinner, Guilfoyle told attendees, including the country’s energy minister, that the U.S. could influence political changes in other countries, which the minister balked at.Per the Journal, Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputed how the dinner unfolded. The Greek government also denied the threat, adding: “Such a thing would never be tolerated.” Marafatsos’s lawyer also contested the Journal’s reporting. Lawyers for Aktor Group denied allegations that Guilfoyle acted improperly in promoting its business interests.Then, on Oct. 7, the Journal reported, citing Guilfoyle’s text messages ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025, that she asked businessman and Trump donor Eric Deters to wire $100,000 to clear her American Express credit card debt in exchange for access to the Trump Administration. Deters, who did not pay Guilfoyle, told the paper that he had transactions with Guilfoyle dating back to 2020. The Journal reported that Deters promised Guilfoyle as much $1 million if she succeeded in helping him connect with the Trump Administration, and that she reportedly offered to use her links as Trump Jr.’s former fiancée. Guilfoyle also reportedly asked Deters to stop creating a paper trail of their dealings. Jesse Binnall, Guilfoyle’s lawyer, told the Journal that the ambassador disputes the messages’ authenticity. He also said that Guilfoyle was paid for events before her nomination and that the ambassador “was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events.”Three days later, the Journal published another report, this time on how Guilfoyle flaunted luxury trips financed by several businessmen, through an audio recording that the paper reviewed. She reportedly acknowledged in the recording that she flew to the January 2026 World Economic Forum on a private jet with Aktor Group’s CEO Alexandros Exarchou. Guilfoyle also reportedly said in the recording that she planned to travel with a Greek shipping magnate, who reportedly also paid for her accommodations.Responding to the Journal’s latest report, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Athens said that Guilfoyle has “faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines.”How are lawmakers reacting?Guilfoyle and the allegations surrounding her add to other issues hounding the Trump Administration heading into the November midterms, where Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in Congress.Some Democrats have called for her removal. In a Sept. 30 letter to Rubio, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D, N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sought answers about the allegations. Meeks said in a statement that the reports about Guilfoyle’s actions were “deeply concerning and suggest potentially corrupt influences on U.S. foreign policy,” adding that if found true, she should be “removed from her position.”Rep. Robert Garcia (D, Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote to Guilfoyle on Oct. 8 that her reported conduct with Deters “raises serious public corruption and national security concerns.” Garcia requested she hand over financial and communications records related to the controversy.Even some top Republicans are concerned: GOP Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming called the reports about Guilfoyle “very troubling.”“I’m sure there’s going to be an investigation,” Barrasso told CBS News Sunday. “I know that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee will have oversight and look into that as well. But I think the public has a right to know what is found, and it is quite a bit of concern.”

items.title: Archbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream execution
items.standfirst: Timothy Broglio says Catholics on army firing squad should ask to be excused since it clashes with church teachingsThe archbishop who oversees the spiritual care of Catholics serving in the US military condemned the Pentagon’s proposed plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan later this year.Archbishop Timothy Broglio also stipulated in a Monday statement that any Catholic soldier assigned to the US army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the live stream plans. Continue reading...
